s: A rod of ten cubes is a *ten*. Ten tens make a *hundred*, which has 100 little cubes.
Look at 347. The 3 is in the hundreds place, so it means 300. The 4 means 4 tens, or 40. The 7 means 7 ones. The place tells the value. A 3 in the ones place is just 3.
m: Money shows place value too. A penny is worth 1 cent. A dime is worth 10 cents. A dollar is worth 100 cents. Ten dimes make one dollar, just as ten tens make one hundred.
Only ten digits, 0 to 9, can write every number. The place a digit sits in does the rest of the work.

s: *Expanded form* stretches a number out. Take 347. It has 3 hundreds, 4 tens and 7 ones. So 347 = 300 + 40 + 7. Add the parts back up to check.
Watch out for zeros. In 508, the 0 means 0 tens. So 508 = 500 + 8, not 58.
m: The zero keeps a place open. In 460, the 0 sits in the ones place. If you left it out, you would have 46, a much smaller number.
Expanded form also shows why place matters. The same digits can make different numbers. 46 is 40 + 6, but 460 is 400 + 60.

s: To read 347, say the hundreds first: three hundred. Then say the rest: forty-seven. Do not say “and” after the hundreds.
Six hundred forty-two is 600 and 42 together: 642. For 803, say eight hundred three. One more than 999 is one *thousand*, written 1,000.
m: The comma in 1,000 is there to help your eye. Later you will see numbers like 12,345. The comma keeps the groups of three digits easy to see.
The digits 0 to 9 that we use today are called Hindu-Arabic numerals. They began in India and came to Europe through the Arab world.

s: Kai has 348 buttons. Rosa has 352. To *compare*, look at the hundreds first. Both have 3 hundreds, so move to the tens. 5 tens is more than 4 tens, so 352 is bigger.
Bigger places win, so start on the left. Check the ones last, only if the hundreds and the tens tie.
m: A dictionary puts words in order the same way. It looks at the first letter, then the second, then the third. Comparing numbers also starts on the left and moves right, one place at a time.
A number with 3 digits, like 100, is bigger than any number with 2 digits, like 99. The first one has a hundreds place and the second does not.

s: Three signs help you compare. The sign > means *greater than*. The sign < means *less than*. The sign = means *equal to*.
The open side of > or < always faces the bigger number, like a hungry mouth. So 352 > 348 and 348 < 352 say the same thing. Two numbers that match get =, like 500 = 500.
m: The equal sign was first used by a Welsh mathematician named Robert Recorde, in 1557. He drew two short lines of the same length, side by side. He felt that nothing could be more equal than two lines like that.

s: To *skip count* is to count by jumps, and each jump adds the same amount. By 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. By 10s: 10, 20, 30, 40. Only the tens digit changes.
By 100s, only the hundreds digit changes. You can start anywhere: 250, 350, 450. Rosa counts 6 cups of 100 buttons: 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600.
m: Skip counting leads to multiplication. Count by 5s six times and you land on 30. Later you will write that as 6 × 5 = 30.
A clock uses it too. The 1 on the clock face means 5 minutes, the 2 means 10 minutes and the 3 means 15 minutes.

s: What is 100 *more* than 462? Add one hundred. The hundreds digit goes from 4 to 5, so it is 562. For 100 *less*, the 4 becomes a 3: 362.
The same trick works for 10, and only the tens digit changes. Be careful with 9 tens. 9 tens plus 1 ten make a new hundred. So 495 + 10 = 505.
m: A number line shows the same idea. Start at 462 and jump 100 to the right. You land on 562. Jump 100 to the left and you land on 362.
You can move two or three hundreds at once. 200 more than 462 is 662, because the hundreds digit goes up by 2.

s: Put 8 buttons in pairs. You get 4 pairs, none left over. So 8 is *even*. Put 7 in pairs. One is left over. So 7 is *odd*.
Look at the ones digit. If it is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8, the number is even. Otherwise it is odd. Even numbers are doubles, like 6 = 3 + 3.
m: Even and odd numbers take turns when you count: 1 is odd, 2 is even, 3 is odd, 4 is even, and so on.
Two even numbers added together make an even number. Two odd numbers added together also make an even number, because the two left-over buttons make a pair.

s: To *add* 32 + 45, break each number apart. 32 is 3 tens and 2 ones. 45 is 4 tens and 5 ones. Add tens with tens: 3 + 4 = 7. Add ones with ones: 2 + 5 = 7. The *sum* is 77.
Never add a ten to a one. In 62 + 15, the 6 and the 1 are both tens, so they go together.
m: You can add the tens first or the ones first. Try 32 + 45 both ways. The answer is the same.
The order of the two numbers does not matter either. 32 + 45 and 45 + 32 both make 77.

s: Add 48 + 36. Ones first: 8 + 6 = 14. That is 1 ten and 4 ones. When you trade ten ones for a ten, you *regroup*. Now add the tens: 4 + 3 = 7, and 1 more from the trade makes 8 tens. So the answer is 84. Forget the traded ten and you get 74.
m: Regrouping works because ten ones and one ten are worth the same amount. Nothing is gained or lost in the trade. You only change how you pile the same blocks.
Coins show it too. Ten pennies are worth the same as one dime. When you swap ten pennies for a dime, you still have the same amount of money.

s: To add 12 + 25 + 18, look for a *friendly pair* that makes a ten. The ones of a friendly pair add to 10, like 2 + 8. So 12 + 18 = 30. Then 30 + 25 = 55.
Add in any order. With four numbers, make two pairs: 21 + 19 = 40 and 14 + 26 = 40. If nothing pairs up, add the tens, then the ones, then trade.
m: A running total helps too. Add two numbers, say the total, and then add the next number to it. That way you hold only one number in your head at a time.
Friendly pairs work with tens as well. 40 and 60 make 100, and so do 30 and 70.

s: To *subtract* 68 − 25, take tens from tens: 6 tens − 2 tens = 4 tens. Then take ones from ones: 8 − 5 = 3. So 68 − 25 = 43. The *difference* is 43. Check by adding the answer back: 43 + 25 = 68.
m: Adding and subtracting are partners that undo each other. If 43 + 25 = 68, then 68 − 25 = 43 and 68 − 43 = 25. These three numbers belong together as a fact family.
You can also count up to subtract. From 25 to 68, go up 20 to reach 45, then 23 more to reach 68. That is 20 + 23 = 43 in all.

s: To subtract 52 − 17, look at the ones. 2 − 7 does not work, because there are not enough ones. So *trade* one ten for ten ones. Now you have 4 tens and 12 ones. 12 − 7 = 5. 4 tens − 1 ten = 3 tens. The answer is 35. Do not flip the ones. Check: 35 + 17 = 52.
m: Trading a ten for ten ones does not change the number. 52 is 5 tens and 2 ones. It is also 4 tens and 12 ones. It is the same amount, written a different way.
Money works the same way. If you have a dime and need to pay 7 cents, you can trade the dime for ten pennies first. Then you pay 7 and still have 3 pennies.

s: To add 235 + 142, add each place alone: 2 + 1 = 3 hundreds, 3 + 4 = 7 tens, 5 + 2 = 7 ones. That is 377. Subtract the same way: 468 − 253 = 215.
Sometimes ten tens trade into the *hundreds place*. In 356 + 271, 5 + 7 = 12 tens, which is 1 hundred and 2 tens. The answer is 627.
m: The same plan works with money. $235 is 2 hundred-dollar bills, 3 ten-dollar bills and 5 one-dollar bills. To add $142, you count each kind of bill by itself.
It helps to estimate first. 235 is close to 240 and 142 is close to 140, so the sum should be near 380. The answer 377 is close, so it makes sense.

s: Rosa sold 48 cups and then 10 more. She uses *mental math*. 48 + 10 = 58. Then 10 more: 68. Only the tens digit changes. With hundreds, only the hundreds digit moves: 325 + 100 = 425. For bigger jumps, count in tens: 76 + 20 is 86, 96. For 483 − 100, the 4 becomes a 3.
m: People use mental math all the time with money. If a snack costs $30 and you have $100, you can think: 10 tens minus 3 tens is 7 tens, so $70 is left.
If you add 10 and then take away 10, you are back where you started. That is a quick way to check your thinking.

s: Kai adds 48 + 36 by jumping: 48 + 30 = 78, then 78 + 6 = 84. This *strategy* works because 36 is 30 and 6. Rosa moves 2 from 36 to 48 and gets 50 + 34 = 84. Moving a part between the numbers keeps the total.
To *explain* a strategy, say what you did and why the total stays. Then check another way. Two different answers mean check again.
m: Think of two plates of cookies. One has 48 and the other has 36. If you move 2 cookies from one plate to the other, there are still 84 cookies in all. Only the plates change.
Another good check is to subtract. If 48 + 36 = 84, then 84 − 36 should give 48. Two different operations that agree make a strong check.
